subject: Measurement invariance (longitudinal): effects coding method. Is my model specification correct?

messages.author: b430763ad49e6cd0
messages.subject: Measurement invariance (longitudinal): effects coding method. Is my model specification correct?
parts:
Dear all,

I would like to know if I am correctly specifying my models in the measurement invariance (MI) analysis. 
If this is correct, then my MI analysis using the standardized factor/LV method is probably wrong. Because when I proceed to the weak invariant model and compare the configural to the weak model, then the degrees of freedom (df) differ for the two methods (i.e. effects coding vs standardization method).

### Configural model

Model1 <- ' 
# latent variables
Motivation0 =~ A1*V_0_1 + B1*V_0_3 + C1*V_0_4 + D1*V_0_5 + E1*V_0_6
Motivation1 =~ A2*V_1_1 + B2*V_1_3 + C2*V_1_4 + D2*V_1_5 + E2*V_1_6
Motivation3 =~ A3*V_3_1 + B3*V_3_3 + C3*V_3_4 + D3*V_3_5 + E3*V_3_6
Motivation4 =~ A4*V_4_1 + B4*V_4_3 + C4*V_4_4 + D4*V_4_5 + E4*V_4_6

# Item covariances

V_0_1 ~~ V_1_1 + V_3_1 + V_4_1
V_1_1 ~~ V_3_1 + V_4_1
V_3_1 ~~ V_4_1 

V_0_3 ~~ V_1_3 + V_3_3 +  V_4_3 
V_1_3 ~~ V_3_3 + V_4_3 
V_3_3 ~~ V_4_3 

V_0_4 ~~ V_1_4 + V_3_4 + V_4_4 
V_1_4 ~~ V_3_4 + V_4_4 
V_3_4 ~~ V_4_4 

V_0_5 ~~ V_1_5 + V_3_5 + V_4_5 
V_1_5 ~~ V_3_5 + V_4_5 
V_3_5 ~~ V_4_5 

V_0_6 ~~ V_1_6 + V_3_6 + V_4_6
V_1_6 ~~ V_3_6 + V_4_6
V_3_6 ~~ V_4_6 

# Factor covariances

Motivation0 ~~ Motivation1 + Motivation3 + Motivation4
Motivation1 ~~ Motivation3 + Motivation4
Motivation3 ~~ Motivation4

# Constraint for effects coding (factor loadings)

A1 + B1 + C1 + D1 + E1 == 5
A2 + B2 + C2 + D2 + E2 == 5
A3 + B3 + C3 + D3 + E3 == 5
A4 + B4 + C4 + D4 + E4 == 5

# Intercepts items

V_0_1 ~ a1*1
V_1_1 ~ a2*1
V_3_1 ~ a3*1
V_4_1 ~ a4*1

V_0_3 ~ b1*1
V_1_3 ~ b2*1
V_3_3 ~ b3*1
V_4_3 ~ b4*1

V_0_4 ~ c1*1
V_1_4 ~ c2*1
V_3_4 ~ c3*1 
V_4_4 ~ c4*1 

V_0_5 ~ d1*1
V_1_5 ~ d2*1
V_3_5 ~ d3*1
V_4_5 ~ d4*1

V_0_6 ~ e1*1
V_1_6 ~ e2*1
V_3_6 ~ e3*1
V_4_6 ~ e4*1

# Constraint for effects coding (intercepts)

a1 + b1 + c1 + d1 + e1 == 0
a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 + e2 == 0
a3 + b3 + c3 + d3 + e3 == 0
a4 + b4 + c4 + d4 + e4 == 0

# Intercepts factors

Motivation0 ~ 1
Motivation1 ~ 1
Motivation3 ~ 1
Motivation4 ~ 1 

'

fit1a <- lavaan(model = Model1, data = data, auto.var = TRUE)
summary(fit1a, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)


#############
## WEAK INVARIANCE (fixed factor loadings over time)
#############

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Measurement invariance (longitudinal): effects coding method. Is my model specification correct?
parts:
Amonet,
  Off the top of my head, I do not see a reason that the df should differ between parameterizations.  In the configural model, each fixed unit loading in the first parameterization corresponds to an effects coding constraint in the second parameterization.  When you impose equality constraints across times, all but one of the fixed unit loadings becomes redundant.  Likewise, all but one of the effects coding constraints becomes redundant.  Everything else should stay the same, unless I am missing something.

  Perhaps it would be best to work with a minimal example, perhaps 2 times and 4 indicators, to work out the conceptual issues.  Then ramp up to the full model once you solve the problem.  It is hard to guess why you are obtaining different df without seeing both parameterizations.  If the reason for the difference does not jump out at you working with smaller models, perhaps you could post just the models that differ in df (presumably either the configural or the weak invariance models) and the df count for each.  That would give us something more concrete with which to work.

Keith

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Measurement invariance (longitudinal): effects coding method. Is my model specification correct?
parts: I would like to know if I am correctly specifying my models in the measurement invariance (MI) analysis.

If this is correct, then my MI analysis using the standardized factor/LV method is probably wrong. Because when I proceed to the weak invariant model and compare the configural to the weak model, then the degrees of freedom (df) differ for the two methods (i.e. effects coding vs standardization method).

When using the standardized-factor method of identification, make sure you free the latent variances for all but 1 time when you constrain loadings across time.  Likewise, when you constrain intercepts across time, you need to free all but one occasion's latent mean.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

parts: I found out about the semTools function longInvariance(), which helped me confirm the results. Very useful function, only it doesn't seem to allow a different baseline / null model in computing the comparative fit indices (such as CFI).

Yeah, not useful enough (only 1 factor, no categorical data). But I just added a baseline.model= argument to each of the invariance functions in the development version of semTools, so you can pass your custom baseline model that way, and it will get passed to fitMeasures() to calculate CFI, etc.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Measurement invariance (longitudinal): effects coding method. Is my model specification correct?
parts:
Oh, and you can install the development versions by running:

install.packages("lavaan", repos="http://www.da.ugent.be", type="source")
devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")
This is the configural model where I manually standardised the four latent variables (Motivation0, Motivation1, 3, 4). Is this normal or known to happen in Lavaan, or am I doing something wrong?

Nothing wrong.  Those are fixed parameters, so don't test them.  It is a numerical machine-precision issue that only happens when you constrain a label to a value (e.g., V==1) instead of fixing it to that value (e.g., Motivation ~~ 1*Motivation).  Sometimes the machine-precision error is large enough (e.g., only 1.000... out to the 15th decimal place instead of the 17th) that the optimizer might stop at a solution a little further away from the exact constraint, but not far enough to be of any practical significance.  That's why you get the same results as setting std.lv = TRUE.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
